title: A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light
gist: Interview with Q.ANT founder-CEO Michael Förtsch on photonic processors positioned as GPU coprocessors for nonlinear AI math, aimed at cutting AI energy and memory-access costs. Q.ANT is piloting chips in IONOS data centers, claims 4-5x energy reduction only in simulation so far, and sees supply chain and developer adoption, not foundry capacity, as the gating constraints.

insights.claim: AI labs and cloud providers are trying to site new data centers in places with cheap renewable energy such as Scandinavia, but logistics, scarcity of key components and anti-data-center protests are slowing that strategy.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Siting constraints on cheap-power data centers raise the value of efficiency-side solutions (chips, cooling) relative to pure power procurement.
insights.locator: To rein in runaway costs, AI labs

insights.claim: Q.ANT CEO Michael Förtsch argues the main cost driver in AI compute today is memory access, so a processor that completes complex math in a single step instead of thousands reduces data movement and therefore energy cost.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Frames AI efficiency as a memory-bandwidth problem; watch architectures that reduce memory traffic as a competitive axis alongside raw FLOPS.
insights.quote: The cost driver today is the access to the memory.
insights.locator: WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining

insights.claim: Photonic processors compute with waves of light instead of moving electrons, which supposedly generates less heat and needs minimal cooling, one of the largest cost sources for data centers.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: If validated, photonics would compress data-center cooling capex/opex, a negative second-order signal for cooling-heavy buildouts.
insights.locator: Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data

insights.claim: Q.ANT positions its photonic chips as coprocessors alongside GPUs rather than replacements: GPUs handle linear math, while photonic processors take complex, nonlinear calculations.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Complementary rather than competitive positioning implies photonics is not a near-term threat to Nvidia's GPU franchise.
insights.quote: Linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.
insights.locator: What distinguishes the type of problem best left

insights.claim: Q.ANT expects photonic processors to be strongest in image and video workloads (recognition, segmentation, generation) and in robotics and physical AI.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Target end-markets for photonic compute adoption are vision and robotics workloads rather than LLM training.
insights.locator: We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures

insights.claim: Q.ANT's claimed four-to-five-times energy reduction from pairing photonic processors with GPUs comes from simulation only and has not yet been demonstrated in real hardware.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Treat photonic efficiency claims as unproven until hardware benchmarks appear from the IONOS pilot.
insights.quote: Under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.
insights.locator: What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency

insights.claim: Förtsch says Q.ANT would not be shy about attacking the GPU directly within five years if an opportunity arises, but that depends on what future AI model architectures and workloads look like.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Long-dated optionality: the coprocessor pitch could turn competitive if model architectures shift toward nonlinear-heavy math.
insights.locator: Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely

insights.claim: Q.ANT has rolled out its photonic chips to data centers operated by cloud company IONOS as a pilot, and says more than 30 engineering teams are developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: IONOS pilot is the first real-world proof point to watch for photonic compute credibility.
insights.locator: Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today

insights.claim: Existing C++ or Python code can run on Q.ANT machines, but GPU-optimized workloads need adaptation to gain speed, creating a chicken-and-egg problem between developer adoption and cloud-provider purchases.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Software ecosystem lock-in (GPU-optimized models) is the main moat incumbents hold against new compute architectures.
insights.locator: It’s a chicken and egg problem, right?

insights.claim: Förtsch says any new processor technology needs time to earn the credibility for a company like Google to build data center infrastructure around it, which is why Q.ANT entered data centers with proof-of-concept systems.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Expect long hyperscaler qualification cycles before photonic chips become material revenue.
insights.locator: Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology

insights.claim: Q.ANT is GPU-vendor agnostic and wants to work alongside both Nvidia and AMD GPUs rather than tying itself to one supplier.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Vendor neutrality widens addressable market but means no single GPU maker will champion the technology.
insights.locator: Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand

insights.claim: Q.ANT photonic chips need only 90-nanometer node technology from the 2000s, letting foundries use existing cheap lines to make higher-priced chips without massive new capital investment, sidestepping the leading-edge capacity crunch.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Photonics could monetize mature-node foundry capacity, a potential tailwind for legacy-node fabs rather than TSMC leading-edge.
insights.quote: you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s
insights.locator: Do you expect to suffer from the same problem

insights.claim: Förtsch says Q.ANT could handle a hypothetical order of 100,000 photonic processors but its suppliers might not, because the photonics assembly supply chain is far less robust than the semiconductor world's.
insights.speaker: Joel Khalili
insights.so_what: Assembly and packaging, not wafer supply, is the scaling bottleneck to monitor for photonic compute.
